title: Bitter taste perception (PTC/PROP) · TAS2R38
summary: TAS2R38 makes a bitter taste receptor. Studies link changes in this gene to sensitivity to bitter test chemicals. This report reads two positions. The common PAV and AVI patterns use three positions, so these readings alone do not establish the full pattern. Sensitivity in a taste test is not the same as liking or disliking a food.

interpretations.CC: Two C copies make Ala49, the non-taster form at this site. On average, this type gives weak or no PTC and PROP taste. It can also make some green vegetables taste less bitter. Food choice still varies widely with culture and habit.
interpretations.CG: One C copy makes Ala49, a non-taster form. One G copy makes Pro49, a taster form. People with CG usually taste PTC and PROP as bitter. On average, the taste is less strong than with GG. It still varies widely among people with CG.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G allele, coding Pro49 on both chromosomes — consistent with the taster (PAV-type) receptor. This genotype is associated on average with strong bitter perception of PTC/PROP and related compounds in some green vegetables. Whether that translates into disliking those foods differs a lot from person to person.

Two G copies code for Ala262, the form at this position in the PAV pattern. That pattern was linked to greater PTC taste sensitivity in the study. This position alone does not establish the full pattern or how strong a taste feels.
interpretations.AG: One G copy codes for Ala262 and one A copy for Val262. These are found in the common PAV and AVI patterns. This reading does not show the full patterns or which changes sit on the same chromosome. It does not give a personal taste score.
interpretations.AA: Two A copies code for Val262, the form at this position in the AVI pattern. That pattern was linked to lower PTC taste sensitivity in the study. This position alone does not establish the full pattern or rule out tasting bitterness.

measured.text: Researchers used a blind taste test to measure the weakest amount of PTC that people could taste. PTC is a bitter test chemical.

population.text: The study included families from Utah. A second sample from NIH included people with European and East Asian ancestry.

comparison.text: Taste scores differed between groups with different three-position gene patterns. People with two PAV patterns had the highest mean scores; those with two AVI patterns had the lowest.

limitation.text: This tested PTC sensitivity, not food choice. The paper compared three-position patterns, not a single letter. This report’s two positions do not establish the full pattern or which changes share one chromosome.
limitation.locator: Pages 1221–1223, measured outcome and three-position analysis; report scope limitation

title: Cilantro tasting like soap · OR6A2 region
summary: A DNA change near smell receptor genes is linked to whether cilantro tastes soapy. OR6A2 is one possible explanation, not a proven cause. The study found a small link, not a test of whether you will enjoy cilantro.

interpretations.CC: Your file shows two C copies. In the study, C was linked to reporting a soapy cilantro taste. This does not mean cilantro must taste soapy to you.
interpretations.AC: Your file shows one A copy. A was linked to less frequent reports of a soapy cilantro taste. The study fitted an average effect per copy, not a measured taste score for you.
interpretations.AA: Your file shows two A copies. A was linked to less frequent reports of a soapy cilantro taste. This does not rule out tasting soap or disliking cilantro.

measured.text: People answered separate questions about a soapy taste and whether they liked fresh cilantro.

population.text: The main study had 14,604 participants of European ancestry. A separate group of 11,851 answered the liking question.
population.locator: Results and Methods; filtered, non-overlapping replication group

comparison.text: The A form was linked to fewer reports of soapiness. The separate liking result was weaker.
comparison.locator: Table 2 and Results, soapiness versus preference

limitation.text: Smelling soap and disliking cilantro are not the same outcome. Nearby genes may explain the link; the study did not prove which one.
limitation.locator: Results and discussion, OR6A2 and OR10A2 candidates

title: Smelling asparagus in urine · OR2M7 region
summary: A DNA region near smell receptor genes is linked to noticing an odor in urine after eating asparagus. The study asked people what they noticed. It did not separately measure their urine or test their sense of smell.

interpretations.AA: Your file shows two A copies. In the study, people with A copies more often reported noticing the odor than people with GG. One and two A copies gave similar results.
interpretations.AG: Your file shows one A copy. In the study, this group more often reported noticing the odor than the GG group. Its result was close to the AA group, not halfway between.
interpretations.GG: Your file shows two G copies. This group less often reported noticing the odor than groups with A copies. Even so, most people with GG in that study said they could smell it.

measured.text: An online survey asked whether people noticed an odor after eating asparagus.

population.text: The study used answers from 4,742 unrelated participants with northern European ancestry.

comparison.text: Groups with one or two A copies more often noticed the odor than the GG group.
comparison.locator: Table 9 and Results, dominant model discussion

limitation.text: Self-reports cannot separate making an odor from detecting it. This position does not measure either process in you.
limitation.locator: Discussion, production versus detection; phenotype question

title: Sneezing in bright light · 2q22 region
summary: Some people sneeze when they move into bright light. A study linked this reflex to a DNA region near ZEB2. It compared survey answers, not a controlled light test. The result describes a group pattern, not a certain response.

interpretations.CC: Your file shows two C copies. This group more often reported sneezing in bright light than the other groups in the study. Most people with CC still reported no reflex.
interpretations.CT: Your file shows one C copy. Reports of sneezing in bright light fell between the CC and TT groups in this study. Your own response may differ.
interpretations.TT: Your file shows two T copies. This group less often reported sneezing in bright light than groups with C copies. Some people with TT still had the reflex.

measured.text: People reported whether bright light made them sneeze.

population.text: The study included 5,390 unrelated participants with northern European ancestry.

comparison.text: The C form was linked to more reports of this reflex. The reflex occurred in every genotype group.

limitation.text: The region is near ZEB2, but the study did not prove that this gene causes the reflex.

title: Earlobe attachment · EDAR
summary: Earlobes are not a simple one-gene trait. Their shape varies on a scale, and many genes play a part. A study of about 74,000 people from several ancestry groups found 49 linked regions. One strong link was the EDAR Val370Ala change, rs3827760. The G copy is common in East Asian and Indigenous American groups but rare elsewhere. It is linked to higher odds of attached earlobes and to small differences in hair, teeth, and ear shape.

interpretations.AA: Two A copies make the Val370 form. This is the usual type in people with European or African ancestry. It is linked to lower odds of attached earlobes at this site. Dozens of other DNA regions shape earlobes, so AA alone tells little.
interpretations.AG: One A and one G allele. The G (Ala370) copy is associated on average with somewhat higher odds of attached or smaller earlobes, along with EDAR's other subtle effects on hair thickness and tooth shape. Earlobe attachment is a continuum, and this is one contributor among many.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G allele (Ala370), very common in East Asian and Indigenous American ancestry. Associated on average with higher odds of attached earlobes and smaller lobes, plus straighter, thicker scalp hair. All of these are average tendencies across populations, not fixed outcomes.

citations.label: Shaffer et al., Am J Hum Genet 2017

title: Wet or dry earwax · ABCC11
summary: A change in ABCC11 is strongly linked to wet or dry earwax. This report checks that common position, not every change in the gene.

interpretations.CC: Your file shows two C copies, the form linked to wet, sticky earwax. This is not a body odor measurement.
interpretations.CT: Your file shows one C and one T copy. The C form is linked to wet earwax even with one copy.
interpretations.TT: Your file shows two T copies, the form linked to dry, flaky earwax. The paper also found a rare change elsewhere in ABCC11.

measured.text: The study compared earwax types and tested gene forms in cells.

population.text: The paper examined wet and dry earwax and compared gene frequencies across populations.

comparison.text: The dry form had lower transport activity in cells.

limitation.text: The cell test did not measure body odor. The paper also found a rare deletion.
limitation.locator: Author abstract; limit of the cell assay

title: Reaction to chewing sounds (misophonia) · TENM2
summary: Misophonia is a very strong negative response to certain daily sounds. Chewing is a common trigger, and some people feel anger or rage. A 23andMe DNA study used one question about rage at eating sounds. It found one strong signal at rs2937573 inside TENM2, a gene active in brain growth. The effect on one person is small. The study used only one self-report question, and few other studies have tested the result. The evidence is therefore early.

interpretations.GG: Two G copies are linked to slightly higher odds of reporting rage at eating sounds. This is one small group link. Most people with GG are not upset by chewing sounds. Many genes and life experiences play a part in true misophonia.
interpretations.AG: One G and one A allele, associated on average with intermediate odds of strong reactions to eating sounds. The per-allele effect found in the study is small, so this genotype says very little about any one person's sound sensitivity.
interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A allele, associated with the lowest average odds at this locus of reporting rage at chewing sounds. People with this genotype can still experience misophonia; this single variant captures only a sliver of the trait.

title: Sprint and power muscle fiber · ACTN3
summary: ACTN3 makes alpha-actinin-3, a protein found only in fast muscle fibers used for sprinting and power. The common R577X change, rs1815739 C>T, can stop the protein from being made. People with TT make none of it, yet this causes no illness. TT occurs in about one in five people with European ancestry. In a well-known study of top Australian athletes, TT was rare among Olympic sprinters. Endurance athletes had it at least as often as other people.

interpretations.CC: Two C copies make Arg577, so both gene copies produce alpha-actinin-3 in fast muscle fibers. CC appears more often among top sprint and power athletes. Some studies also link it to slightly better sprint results. For one person, training history matters far more than this DNA site.
interpretations.CT: One C copy works, and one T copy stops early. The body still makes alpha-actinin-3. In group studies, CT falls between CC and TT on sprint measures. The differences are too small to notice outside top-level sport.
interpretations.TT: Two T copies make the R577X stop form, so the body makes no alpha-actinin-3. A related protein, alpha-actinin-2, takes its place. TT was rare among top sprinters in athlete studies. On average, it is linked to slightly less muscle power and perhaps better endurance economy. It has no known health effect, and many strong, fast people have TT.

citations.label: Yang et al., Am J Hum Genet 2003

title: Androstenone smell perception · OR7D4
summary: Androstenone is a chemical in sweat and boar meat. To some people, it smells very bad. Others find it faint, sweet, or have no smell at all. Much of this difference comes from the OR7D4 smell receptor. The rs61729907 change makes Arg88Trp and marks the weaker WM receptor form. This form usually travels with the Thr133Met change. It weakens the receptor's response. On average, carriers find the smell less strong and less unpleasant.

interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G (Arg88) allele — the fully functional RT form of OR7D4 on both chromosomes. On average this genotype is associated with perceiving androstenone as more intense and more unpleasant (sweaty, urinous). Perception still varies with overall olfactory sensitivity and other receptor genes.
interpretations.AG: One G copy makes the working receptor, and one A copy makes the weaker Trp88 form. In the first study, AG rated the smell as much less strong and less unpleasant than GG on average. This shows how one smell receptor can shift odor experience.
interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A (Trp88) allele, consistent with the impaired WM receptor on both chromosomes. Associated on average with reduced sensitivity to androstenone; some people with this genotype describe it as faint, sweet, or vanilla-like, or cannot smell it at all. A harmless perceptual difference.

title: Sweet taste perception · TAS1R3
summary: TAS1R3 makes half of the main receptor for sweet taste. Two changes in its control region are rs35744813, shown here, and the closely linked rs307355. In lab tests, the T copies lowered how strongly the gene switched on. In taste tests, they were linked to lower sensitivity to sucrose. Together, they explained up to about 16% of the differences in that study. The evidence comes mainly from one strong study with lab follow-up, so it is still early.

interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele, the version shown to lower TAS1R3 promoter activity. Associated on average with reduced sensitivity to low concentrations of sucrose — needing a bit more sugar to notice sweetness. This is a subtle threshold shift, not a change in liking sweet foods, which is shaped by many factors.
interpretations.CT: One T and one C copy gave a middle level of sweet taste sensitivity in the first study. Context, food temperature, and repeated exposure affect daily sweet taste far more than this DNA type.
interpretations.CC: Two C copies make the more active control form. On average, CC could detect sweetness in weaker sugar water. T copies are much more common in people with African ancestry. This helps explain average ancestry-linked differences at this site.
